source: cook_fb_1895_2, printed p134, one-based PDF150, editorial prose lines1–7, ending before Ðonne cwīð se
translation: Indeed, the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels together with him to the great judgment. Then he sits on the throne of his majesty, and all nations are gathered before him, and he separates them into two groups, just as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Then he places the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left.
observations: The scene is prospective: English will come, will sit, will be gathered, will separate and will place may consistently express its reference. Old English present morphology is not an automatic future auxiliary construction.
The angels phrase has an understood coming predicate. It is not another overt finite verb and not the object of mid; him is that preposition's complement.
There are six overt finite predicates: cymð, sitt, bēoð, tōscǣt twice, and gelōgað. Bēoð belongs with the following nominative plural ealle ðēoda and the supplied participle gegaderode.
Mægenðrymnesse is genitive within the dative throne phrase. Cook's own note refers to §153.f; this does not turn the throne into a genitive.
Both Ðonne occurrences sequence the scene as then. Swā-swā introduces the supplied comparison.
Scēap is accusative plural in both relevant object phrases, despite the identical singular surface. Gātum is dative plural after fram; gǣt is accusative plural.

Swīðran and winstran have syncretic weak feminine endings. Bare hand and the construction support the accusative right/left-side idiom. The following unassigned source sentence also uses on his swīðran hand with standað, so a directional-only explanation is insufficient. The last hand is understood.
The original wording, including ęnglas, ðǣm, miclan, swā-swā, scēaphierde, scēap and gǣt, must remain distinct from normalized new teaching material.
